 PORTLAND, Ore. (KATU) — The U.S. Attorney for the District of Oregon is set to reveal what it calls major updates on efforts to fight SNAP benefit theft. 
 Scott E. Bradford, U.S. Attorney for the District of Oregon, is set to discuss the Supplemental Nutritional Assistance Program (or SNAP) at a press conference on Wednesday at 1 p.m.
 Livestream is starting soon 
 Bradford said his office will announce “major developments in the office’s ongoing efforts to combat large scale theft of SNAP benefits.” 
 The announcement comes amid several changes within the food assistance program. In Oregon, SNAP recipients recently saw a small increase in monthly payments to keep pace with rising grocery prices.
 Under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, states must now cover 75% of SNAP administrative costs, adding millions of dollars in new expenses to state budgets. The law also includes more stringent work requirements for able-bodied adults without dependents through age 64, and removes an exemption for families with children age 14 and older.
 PAST COVERAGE | Major changes to SNAP benefits took effect on Oct. 1. Here's what you need to know. 
 There are just under 640,000 Oregonians who get SNAP benefits, according to the state Department of Human Services, with that number down 9% since July of 2025.
 Also under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, states with SNAP error rates higher than 6% could face penalties starting in 2027, and would have to cover some of the benefit costs themselves. The so-called Payment Error Rate looks at when a state overpays or underpays recipients. State officials said that rate is not intended to measure fraud in the system, but keep payments accurate.
 According to data from the USDA , Oregon’s Payment Error Rate was 14.14% in 2025. 
 Along with Wednesday's announcement from the Oregon U.S. Attorney's Office, Vice President JD Vance, U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche and others announced findings from what they said was the first nationwide surge focusing on SNAP fraud.
 Vance says they've uncovered $42 million in SNAP fraud just since September. Officials said they've indicted people in 13 districts and will continue.
